CCPA EMPLOYEE AND JOB APPLICANT DATA — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc. · privacy@acme.com or (415) 555-0100

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This CCPA Employee and Job Applicant Data — Information Sheet describes how the California Consumer Privacy Act, as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act (California Civil Code § 1798.100 et seq.), applies to personal information Acme, Inc. collects and maintains about its own personnel — job applicants, current and former employees, and other personnel described in this information sheet — as distinct from personal information Acme, Inc. collects from its customers or website visitors. A job applicant, employee, or other personnel with questions about this information sheet, or who wishes to exercise a right described in it, may contact Acme, Inc. as follows: privacy@acme.com or (415) 555-0100. This information sheet does not itself set out the consumer-facing privacy notice Acme, Inc. provides to its customers or website visitors, or the contract terms between Acme, Inc. and any vendor or service provider that processes personal information on Acme, Inc.'s behalf; those are addressed in separate documents.

THE FORMER, TEMPORARY EMPLOYEE/HR DATA EXEMPTION HAS EXPIRED
When California's Consumer Privacy Act was first enacted, it included two temporary, limited exemptions — codified as subdivisions (m) and (n) of Civil Code § 1798.145 — under which personal information a business collected about its own job applicants, employees, owners, directors, officers, medical staff members, or independent contractors, solely within the context of that role, was not subject to most of the Act's obligations, and a similar, narrower exemption applied to personal information reflecting a business-to-business communication or transaction with a natural person acting on behalf of another company, partnership, sole proprietorship, nonprofit, or government agency. Both of these exemptions were, by their own statutory terms, temporary: each subdivision states that it became inoperative on January 1, 2023. That expiration is not merely a historical footnote — it is recorded in the official history note appended to the current, in-force version of § 1798.145 (as most recently amended effective January 1, 2024), which states plainly that 'Subdivisions (m) and (n) inoperative January 1, 2023, by their own provisions.' The text of subdivisions (m) and (n) still appears in the printed statute, but neither has had any legal effect since January 1, 2023. As a result, and subject to the Act's other, non-employment-specific exemptions and exceptions, personal information a business collects about its own job applicants, employees, and other personnel has been fully subject to the CCPA/CPRA's general framework — the same framework that applies to a business's customers — since that date.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(m) (1) This title shall not apply to any of the following:(A) Personal information that is collected by a business about a natural person in the course of the natural person acting as a job applicant to, an employee of, owner of, director of, officer of, medical staff member of, or independent contractor of, that business to the extent that the natural person’s personal information is collected and used by the business solely within the context of the natural person’s role or former role as a job applicant to, an employee of, owner of, director of, officer of, medical staff member of, or an independent contractor of, that business."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.145(m)(1)(A) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), Former CCPA exemption for personal information collected about a business's own job applicants, employees, and other personnel (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.145.)
  "(4) This subdivision shall become inoperative on January 1, 2023."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.145(m)(4) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), Sunset date of the former job-applicant/employee/personnel exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.145.)
  "(n) (1) The obligations imposed on businesses by Sections 1798.100, 1798.105, 1798.106, 1798.110, 1798.115, 1798.121, 1798.130, and 1798.135 shall not apply to personal information reflecting a written or verbal communication or a transaction between the business and the consumer, where the consumer is a natural person who acted or is acting as an employee, owner, director, officer, or independent contractor of a company, partnership, sole proprietorship, nonprofit, or government agency and whose communications or transaction with the business occur solely within the context of the business conducting due diligence regarding, or providing or receiving a product or service to or from such company, partnership, sole proprietorship, nonprofit, or government agency."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.145(n)(1) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), Former, related business-to-business personal information exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.145.)
  "(3) This subdivision shall become inoperative on January 1, 2023."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.145(n)(3) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), Sunset date of the former business-to-business personal information exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.145.)
  "(Amended by Stats. 2023, Ch. 567, Sec. 2. (AB 1194) Effective January 1, 2024. Subdivisions (m) and (n) inoperative January 1, 2023, by their own provisions.)"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.145, official history/amendment note (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), Current statute's own confirmation that subdivisions (m) and (n) are inoperative as of January 1, 2023 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.145.)

This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CCPA/CPRA framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer; other states now have their own, differently structured privacy and employment statutes, and this document addresses California's CCPA/CPRA only. This clause does not separately quote or verify subdivision (m)(1)(B) and (C) (the former exemption's narrower emergency-contact-information and benefits-administration carve-outs) or the full text of subdivision (n)(1) beyond what is quoted in this document's citations, though (n)(1) is quoted in full among this clause's citations; both former exemptions are, in any event, equally inoperative as of January 1, 2023. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text, including its own history note, is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

A BUSINESS'S OWN PERSONNEL CAN BE “CONSUMERS” UNDER THE ACT'S GENERAL DEFINITION
The CCPA/CPRA defines “consumer,” for purposes of the entire title, broadly: a natural person who is a California resident, however identified, including by any unique identifier. Nothing in that general definition turns on whether the natural person is a customer, a website visitor, or instead a job applicant, employee, or other person who performs services for the business. Before January 1, 2023, a job applicant's, employee's, or other personnel's status as such was addressed separately, through the now-inoperative exemption described elsewhere in this information sheet. With that exemption no longer in effect, a business's own personnel who are California residents fall within the Act's general “consumer” definition on the same terms as anyone else, so that personal information a business collects and maintains about them is, subject to the Act's other, non-employment-specific exemptions and exceptions, personal information about a consumer for purposes of the title.

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(i) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Consumer Privacy Act, definition of “consumer” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.140.)

This clause does not itself determine whether any specific job applicant, employee, or other individual is in fact a California resident within the meaning of the cross-referenced regulation, which is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve. This clause also does not restate the Act's other, non-employment-specific exemptions and exceptions (for example, the deidentified/aggregate information exemption or the evidentiary-privilege limitation in § 1798.145), which continue to apply to personal information about personnel on the same terms they apply to any other consumer's personal information and were not independently verified for this clause. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

WHICH EMPLOYERS ARE SUBJECT TO THESE OBLIGATIONS
The obligations described in this information sheet apply only to an entity that meets the CCPA/CPRA's own definition of a “business.” Among other structural requirements — including that the entity is organized or operated for the profit or financial benefit of its shareholders or other owners, collects consumers' personal information (or has it collected on the entity's behalf), determines the purposes and means of processing that personal information, and does business in California — the statute requires that the entity satisfy at least one of three numerical thresholds: annual gross revenue in excess of $25,000,000 in the preceding calendar year; annually buying, selling, or sharing the personal information of 100,000 or more consumers or households, alone or in combination; or deriving 50 percent or more of its annual revenue from selling or sharing consumers' personal information. An entity that does not meet the statutory definition of a “business” is not, on that basis, subject to the obligations this information sheet describes with respect to personal information about its own personnel, regardless of whether the now-inoperative employee/personnel exemption discussed elsewhere in this information sheet would otherwise have applied.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(d)(1) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Consumer Privacy Act, definition of “business” and its revenue/volume thresholds (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.140.)

This clause does not restate § 1798.140(d)(2) through (4), which extend the “business” definition to certain affiliated entities sharing common branding, certain joint ventures and partnerships, and entities that voluntarily certify compliance with the title; those provisions were reviewed as part of the same fetched section but are not separately quoted or detailed here because they are narrower extensions of, rather than substitutes for, the general threshold test quoted in this clause. This clause does not determine whether any specific employer in fact meets one of these thresholds, which is a fact-specific financial and operational question this document does not resolve. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

THE NOTICE-AT-COLLECTION REQUIREMENT APPLIES TO PERSONAL INFORMATION COLLECTED FROM PERSONNEL
California law requires that a business that controls the collection of a consumer's personal information inform consumers, at or before the point of collection, of the categories of personal information to be collected and the purposes for which those categories are collected or used, and whether that information is sold or shared; a business may not then collect additional categories of personal information, or use personal information for additional purposes, that are incompatible with the disclosed purpose, without providing a further notice consistent with this requirement. Because a business's own job applicants, employees, and other personnel who are California residents are “consumers” under the Act's general definition, and because the former exemption that once excused a business from most CCPA obligations toward personal information collected in that context is now inoperative, this notice-at-collection requirement applies to personal information a business collects from its personnel in the same way it applies to personal information the business collects from its customers. The statute imposes parallel content requirements — addressed elsewhere in the same section — for sensitive personal information and for disclosing the length of time, or the criteria for determining the length of time, a business intends to retain each category of personal information.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(a) A business that controls the collection of a consumer’s personal information shall, at or before the point of collection, inform consumers of the following:(1) The categories of personal information to be collected and the purposes for which the categories of personal information are collected or used and whether that information is sold or shared. A business shall not collect additional categories of personal information or use personal information collected for additional purposes that are incompatible with the disclosed purpose for which the personal information was collected without providing the consumer with notice consistent with this section."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100(a)(1) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Consumer Privacy Act, point-of-collection notice content requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.100.)

This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CCPA/CPRA framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer; other states now have their own, differently structured privacy and employment statutes, and this document addresses California's CCPA/CPRA only. This clause quotes only paragraph (1) of subdivision (a); it does not separately quote paragraphs (2) (the parallel sensitive-personal-information notice content) and (3) (the retention-period disclosure) of the same subdivision, or subdivision (b) (the alternative homepage-posting method available to a third party that controls collection, which is unlikely to be the applicable method for personnel-directed notices and was not evaluated for that context) — the full text of subdivision (a) and (b) is independently verified and quoted in this corpus's existing CCPA consumer-facing privacy policy document, which addresses the same statutory section from the customer-facing side. This clause does not determine, for any specific business, the actual categories of personal information collected from personnel, the purposes of that collection, or the retention period the business intends — those are fact-specific determinations left to the drafting portion of this information sheet. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

THE RIGHTS TO KNOW, DELETE, AND CORRECT PERSONAL INFORMATION NOW APPLY TO PERSONNEL DATA
California law gives a consumer the right to request that a business delete personal information the business has collected from the consumer; the right to request that a business that maintains inaccurate personal information about the consumer correct that inaccurate personal information, taking into account the nature of the personal information and the purposes of processing it; and the right to request that a business that collects personal information about the consumer disclose the categories of personal information it has collected, the categories of sources, the business or commercial purpose for collecting it, the categories of third parties to whom it is disclosed, and the specific pieces of personal information collected about that consumer. Because the former exemption for personal information collected in the job-applicant, employee, or other personnel context is now inoperative, these three rights apply, on the same terms described in this section, to personal information a business maintains about a current or former job applicant, employee, or other personnel described in this information sheet — for example, information in a personnel file, application materials, or performance or compensation records — to the extent that information is personal information about a California-resident natural person within the meaning of the Act. The Act's other consumer rights (including the rights to know what personal information is sold or shared and to whom, to opt out of sale or sharing, and to limit use of sensitive personal information) and its non-discrimination provision likewise apply to personnel on the same general terms they apply to any other consumer, though this clause addresses only the right to know, delete, and correct.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(a) A consumer shall have the right to request that a business delete any personal information about the consumer which the business has collected from the consumer."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.105(a) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Consumer Privacy Act, consumer's right to delete personal information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.105.)
  "(a) A consumer shall have the right to request a business that maintains inaccurate personal information about the consumer to correct that inaccurate personal information, taking into account the nature of the personal information and the purposes of the processing of the personal information."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.106(a) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Consumer Privacy Act, consumer's right to correct inaccurate personal information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.106.)
  "(a) A consumer shall have the right to request that a business that collects personal information about the consumer disclose to the consumer the following:(1) The categories of personal information it has collected about that consumer.(2) The categories of sources from which the personal information is collected.(3) The business or commercial purpose for collecting, selling, or sharing personal information.(4) The categories of third parties to whom the business discloses personal information.(5) The specific pieces of personal information it has collected about that consumer."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.110(a) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Consumer Privacy Act, consumer's right to know what personal information is collected and to access it (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.110.)

This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CCPA/CPRA framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer; other states now have their own, differently structured privacy and employment statutes, and this document addresses California's CCPA/CPRA only. This clause does not restate the statutory exceptions to the deletion right (Civil Code § 1798.105(d)), which permit a business to decline a deletion request for reasons such as completing a transaction, security, debugging, legal compliance, and certain other statutory grounds, and which apply to a request from personnel on the same terms they apply to a request from any other consumer; those exceptions were not independently quoted or verified for this clause. No case law was checked on any of these three provisions; each statute's own text is unambiguous, so the statutes stand as the source here without a corroborating case.

NOTICE AT COLLECTION — CATEGORIES AND PURPOSES FOR PERSONNEL PERSONAL INFORMATION
At or before the point Acme, Inc. collects personal information from a job applicant, employee, or other personnel described in this information sheet, Acme, Inc. discloses the following categories of personal information collected: Identifiers (name, contact info), employment history, education, and performance records. Acme, Inc. collects and uses those categories of personal information for the following purposes: Recruiting, payroll and benefits administration, and performance management. Acme, Inc. does not collect additional categories of personal information, or use personal information collected for additional purposes, that are incompatible with the purposes disclosed above without providing a further notice. A job applicant, employee, or other personnel with questions about this notice, or who wishes to submit a request to exercise a right described in this information sheet, may contact Acme, Inc. as follows: privacy@acme.com or (415) 555-0100.

Executed on September 3, 2026 at Oakland, California.

expectedJSON.body: The obligations described in this information sheet apply only to an entity that meets the CCPA/CPRA's own definition of a “business.” Among other structural requirements — including that the entity is organized or operated for the profit or financial benefit of its shareholders or other owners, collects consumers' personal information (or has it collected on the entity's behalf), determines the purposes and means of processing that personal information, and does business in California — the statute requires that the entity satisfy at least one of three numerical thresholds: annual gross revenue in excess of $25,000,000 in the preceding calendar year; annually buying, selling, or sharing the personal information of 100,000 or more consumers or households, alone or in combination; or deriving 50 percent or more of its annual revenue from selling or sharing consumers' personal information. An entity that does not meet the statutory definition of a “business” is not, on that basis, subject to the obligations this information sheet describes with respect to personal information about its own personnel, regardless of whether the now-inoperative employee/personnel exemption discussed elsewhere in this information sheet would otherwise have applied.

expectedJSON.body: California law requires that a business that controls the collection of a consumer's personal information inform consumers, at or before the point of collection, of the categories of personal information to be collected and the purposes for which those categories are collected or used, and whether that information is sold or shared; a business may not then collect additional categories of personal information, or use personal information for additional purposes, that are incompatible with the disclosed purpose, without providing a further notice consistent with this requirement. Because a business's own job applicants, employees, and other personnel who are California residents are “consumers” under the Act's general definition, and because the former exemption that once excused a business from most CCPA obligations toward personal information collected in that context is now inoperative, this notice-at-collection requirement applies to personal information a business collects from its personnel in the same way it applies to personal information the business collects from its customers. The statute imposes parallel content requirements — addressed elsewhere in the same section — for sensitive personal information and for disclosing the length of time, or the criteria for determining the length of time, a business intends to retain each category of personal information.

citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, point-of-collection notice content requirement
citations.quote: (a) A business that controls the collection of a consumer’s personal information shall, at or before the point of collection, inform consumers of the following:(1) The categories of personal information to be collected and the purposes for which the categories of personal information are collected or used and whether that information is sold or shared. A business shall not collect additional categories of personal information or use personal information collected for additional purposes that are incompatible with the disclosed purpose for which the personal information was collected without providing the consumer with notice consistent with this section.

expectedJSON.body: California law gives a consumer the right to request that a business delete personal information the business has collected from the consumer; the right to request that a business that maintains inaccurate personal information about the consumer correct that inaccurate personal information, taking into account the nature of the personal information and the purposes of processing it; and the right to request that a business that collects personal information about the consumer disclose the categories of personal information it has collected, the categories of sources, the business or commercial purpose for collecting it, the categories of third parties to whom it is disclosed, and the specific pieces of personal information collected about that consumer. Because the former exemption for personal information collected in the job-applicant, employee, or other personnel context is now inoperative, these three rights apply, on the same terms described in this section, to personal information a business maintains about a current or former job applicant, employee, or other personnel described in this information sheet — for example, information in a personnel file, application materials, or performance or compensation records — to the extent that information is personal information about a California-resident natural person within the meaning of the Act. The Act's other consumer rights (including the rights to know what personal information is sold or shared and to whom, to opt out of sale or sharing, and to limit use of sensitive personal information) and its non-discrimination provision likewise apply to personnel on the same general terms they apply to any other consumer, though this clause addresses only the right to know, delete, and correct.

citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, consumer's right to delete personal information
citations.quote: (a) A consumer shall have the right to request that a business delete any personal information about the consumer which the business has collected from the consumer.

citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, consumer's right to correct inaccurate personal information
citations.quote: (a) A consumer shall have the right to request a business that maintains inaccurate personal information about the consumer to correct that inaccurate personal information, taking into account the nature of the personal information and the purposes of the processing of the personal information.

citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, consumer's right to know what personal information is collected and to access it
citations.quote: (a) A consumer shall have the right to request that a business that collects personal information about the consumer disclose to the consumer the following:(1) The categories of personal information it has collected about that consumer.(2) The categories of sources from which the personal information is collected.(3) The business or commercial purpose for collecting, selling, or sharing personal information.(4) The categories of third parties to whom the business discloses personal information.(5) The specific pieces of personal information it has collected about that consumer.
